name: Wei Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wei. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an electric rope shovel at an oil sands mine, the big machine that digs the sand and loads it into the haul trucks. The bucket takes about a hundred tonnes a pass, and it's four passes to fill a truck. I fly in for seven days and out for seven, and on shift it's twelve hours in the cab with a thermos and a lot of concentration. The skill is in loading the truck evenly and fast without banging the bucket on the box, and on a good day I'm the fastest on the crew. The cold in January and the camp food are what wear me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's life like on your weeks off?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Lin does the books for a car dealership, so I cook on my off weeks to give her a break. Our daughter Mei is a civil engineer and our son Karl runs a bike shop, both grown and out of the house. I fish when I can. I use the AI chat thing now and then, mostly to check pension rules or to plan a fishing trip, once my son-in-law showed me it wasn't too hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, one less thing to worry about. Some of it's useful, like the faster maintenance reports, and the rest was talk. I'm not one for posting, but I'd say that much at camp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my plan stays my plan. I work to sixty-five in 2033, take the company pension, and fish. That's been the target for ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. I'd keep running the shovel, keep saving my bit each month into the pension top-up, and maybe use the AI thing a little more for paperwork. Nothing worth spending money on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Monday at camp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some of it's useful. What's an example from your mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The maintenance crew uses it to sort out which shovel part is likely to fail next. Last spring it flagged a cracked boom weld on the shovel next to mine a week before anyone saw it. That's good, and it didn't cost anyone a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oil prices, mostly. That's what really decides whether this mine runs at full tilt or cuts a crew. AI or no AI, that's the thing I watch.

S0.say: Fine, good, one less thing to worry about. Some of it's useful, like faster maintenance reports, and the rest was talk.
S0.think: My plan stays my plan: I work to sixty-five in 2033, take the company pension and fish. That's been the target for ten years.
S0.do: Keeps running the shovel and saving his monthly pension top-up. Uses the AI program a bit more for paperwork and spends nothing extra.
S0.feel: Calm, like a normal Monday at camp.
S0.quote: Last spring it flagged a cracked boom weld on the shovel next to mine a week before anyone saw it.
S0.fieldNote: Wei is a numbers person who has had the same retirement target for a decade. He sees useful sides to the technology and judges it by whether it costs jobs. Oil prices, not AI, are his long-standing worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming and people should get ready, not panic. The company should offer training and the government should help those who get hit hardest. That's fair to everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the shovel is one of the last machines they'll automate. The trucks I load will go driverless first, they're already doing it at the mine up the road. As long as I'm the one filling them, I've got work to 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the shovel and put my hand up if they trial assisted digging, where the computer helps steer the bucket. I'd spend an evening or two on my off week learning the AI tools properly, since it's clearly not going away. And I'd keep the same savings plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A bit curious, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truck drivers, especially the younger ones who just bought houses. Kirsty on my crew bought a place in town last year with a big mortgage. I'd tell her to get into the control room training early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try the assisted digging. Would that be hard for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, at first, like any new machine. But I've learned three different shovel models in thirty years. If the guy next to me is getting good results with it, I'd want to know why.

S1.say: Change is coming and people should get ready, not panic. The company should offer training and the government should help those hit hardest.
S1.think: The shovel is one of the last machines they'll automate, while the trucks I load go driverless first. As long as I'm the one filling them, I've got work to 2033.
S1.do: Keeps running the shovel and volunteers for any trial of computer-assisted digging. Spends a couple of evenings learning AI tools properly and keeps his savings plan unchanged.
S1.quote: If the guy next to me is getting good results with it, I'd want to know why.
S1.fieldNote: Wei reads the order of automation carefully and puts his shovel near the end of the line. He's willing to try new systems once peers show they work, which fits his steady habits. His concern goes to younger truck drivers with mortgages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready for this, not the company, not the government, not us. We'd need quick help for families, whatever it costs. I'd say it at camp and at the dinner table, but I wouldn't be marching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be sixty in 2028, which is the earliest the company pension lets me go, with a cut of about a fifth. So I have an exit door, it's just smaller than I wanted. With maybe four months in the bank, I'd take it and not wait around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd ask the pension office for exact numbers on going at sixty. We'd cut back hard, no new truck, no fishing lodge trip, and push savings toward six months. Then I'd retire the day I could rather than wait to be let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared out of my mind, but the plan I spent ten years on gets cut by a fifth overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lin that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show her the pension sheet and say, here's the worst case and here's how we live on it. She's the bookkeeper, she'd find the holes in my maths in five minutes. Then we'd work out whether her job's safe, because the dealership might get hit too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new truck I've been eyeing, then the boat upgrade. Probably the cabin trip with the grandkids too, which would hurt more than the truck. Food and the mortgage-free house we'd keep, thank God that's paid off.

S2.say: Nobody's ready for this, not the company, not the government, not us. We'd need quick help for families, whatever it costs.
S2.think: I'd be sixty, the earliest the company pension lets me go, with a cut of about a fifth. I have an exit door, it's just smaller than I wanted, and with four months saved I'd take it.
S2.do: Asks the pension office for exact numbers on retiring at sixty. Cuts back hard on the new truck and trips, pushes savings toward six months, and retires as soon as he can rather than wait to be let go.
S2.feel: Anxious that ten years of planning gets cut by a fifth overnight, but not terrified.
S2.quote: I have an exit door, it's just smaller than I wanted.
S2.fieldNote: Wei's earliest pension age lands exactly in 2028, which gives him an option most workers wouldn't have. He handles the shock with spreadsheets and his wife's bookkeeping eye. The loss he feels most is not money but the cabin trip with his grandchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people start now. Companies should be upfront about their timelines so workers can make choices. I'd say that at the next town hall at camp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, 2031 means I'd be sixty-three. I'd probably work until the shovel's automated, then go with a smaller cut than in the fast one. It's not perfect, but it's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as normal for the first couple of years and watch what the mine actually does. I'd boost savings by about two hundred a month so the gap to sixty-five is easier. If they offered training on the remote shovel, I'd take it once a few others had tried it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a shadow on the plan, but the plan still works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is it different from 2028 for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I go at sixty because I have to. In 2031 I go at sixty-three because I choose to. The money's better and so is the feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mei or Karl be affected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mei designs roads and bridges, and I honestly don't know if AI takes that. Karl fixes bikes, and I'd guess people will want a person for that a while longer. I'd ask them both, but they'd probably know more than me.

S3.say: Five years is enough to plan if people start now. Companies should be upfront about their timelines so workers can make choices.
S3.think: I'd be sixty-three in 2031, so I'd work until the shovel's automated and then go with a smaller pension cut than in the fast one. It's not perfect, but it's manageable.
S3.do: Keeps going as normal for the first couple of years while watching what the mine does. Adds about two hundred a month to savings and would take remote shovel training once others had tried it.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with a shadow over a plan that still works.
S3.quote: In 2028 I go at sixty because I have to. In 2031 I go at sixty-three because I choose to.
S3.fieldNote: Three extra years turn a forced exit into a choice for Wei, and he values that more than the extra money. He remains a careful watcher rather than an early mover. He's honest that he doesn't know what his children's work will look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent warning, so people should use it. Get training, pay down debts, don't wait for someone else to fix it. And the government should have a plan ready for those it does hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, I'm out in 2033 with my full pension, so it doesn't change much. The robots would arrive after I've hung up my hard hat. I'd mostly be curious to see what the mine looks like without us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the shovel and stick to the plan. Maybe I'd try the remote shovel if they trialled it before I left, just to say I'd done it. Otherwise it's the same savings, the same fishing trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Almost relieved, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said relieved. Relieved about what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the timing works out for me. My dad lost his job at the steel mill at fifty-seven and never really got back on his feet. I always swore that wouldn't be me, and in this picture it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell young people to start in mining in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to go in with eyes open. Do a few years, make good money, but learn something on the side, maybe electrical or controls. Don't plan on a thirty-year career on a shovel like I had.

S4.say: Ten years is a decent warning, so people should use it to train and pay down debts instead of waiting for someone else to fix it. The government should have a plan for those it hits.
S4.think: I'm out in 2033 with my full pension, so it doesn't change much, and the robots arrive after I've hung up my hard hat. I'd mostly be curious to see the mine without us.
S4.do: Keeps running the shovel and sticks to his retirement plan. Might try a remote shovel trial before leaving, and keeps the same savings and fishing trips.
S4.feel: Calm, almost relieved that the timing works out.
S4.quote: My dad lost his job at the steel mill at fifty-seven and never really got back on his feet.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Wei is safe, and the relief traces back to his father losing work late in life. His advice to young people is practical: earn well, but learn a second skill. He balances personal responsibility with a role for government, in keeping with his centre views.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it forces me out at sixty with a fifth cut off my pension. What would help is a top-up for people pushed out early by automation, so the pension isn't cut just because the machines came three years too soon.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how long it takes to become good at this. It took me eight years before I could load a truck in four clean passes every time. A robot might do it in a month, but there's a lot of quiet pride in those eight years, and nobody puts that on a spreadsheet.

headlineQuote: It took me eight years before I could load a truck in four clean passes every time.
portrait: Wei Bauer is a 58-year-old rope shovel operator at an oil sands mine who works seven days on, seven off, and has planned for a decade to retire at sixty-five with a company pension. He is pragmatic, a careful planner, and picks up new tools once others have shown they work. He is calm through the plateau and steady change, reasoning that shovels will be among the last machines automated. AGI by 2028 makes him anxious because he'd have to leave at sixty with a reduced pension, while five years leaves him uneasy and ten years leaves him calm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would force him out at sixty with about a fifth cut from his pension.
whatWouldHelp: A pension top-up for workers pushed out early by automation, so their pension isn't cut because the machines came too soon.
